title: The force of imagination
hook: imagination can make us ill or well (Essays 1.21)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was different roads: sometimes pity softens a conqueror, sometimes courage. Your line was different roads.

A passenger on a plane starts scratching their head. Two minutes later, the passenger behind them is scratching too. Nothing has landed on that second head. Only a picture in a mind has changed. Or someone at dinner describes a dentist's drill in detail, and around the table, jaws clench. Montaigne noticed this in himself and gave it an essay, which opens on a Latin saying of the scholars: a strong imagination produces the event.
screen: `AN ITCH ON A PLANE.` → `THE ROW BEHIND STARTS TOO.` → `A PICTURE DID THAT.`

segments.voice: First, the confession. Montaigne says plainly that he's one of the people imagination works on hardest. The sight of someone else's pain gives him a pain of his own. A man who keeps coughing near him makes his own lungs and throat feel raw. It isn't a theory. It's a report on his body. Second, the pin. He tells of a woman who was sure she'd swallowed a pin with her bread, and cried out that she could feel it stuck in her throat. Someone sensible guessed it was her imagination, made her throw up, and slipped a bent pin into what came up. Seeing it, she felt her pain lift. Third, the doctors. Physicians work on a patient's imagination too, Montaigne notes, winning belief with promises of a cure, so that imagination can do part of the work. In this essay, imagination can make us ill, and it can help make us well. Fourth, his honesty about his stories. He admits he can't vouch for every tale he borrows, and leaves them on the conscience of whoever told them. What matters to him is that they're possible, and that they show something true about how people are made. It's a careful line, and it fits the subject: an author who knows his own mind can run ahead of the facts. In a plain week, the force of imagination is the email you've decided is angry before you open it. Montaigne's move is to notice: the mind is making a picture, and the body is believing it.
screen: `HE FEELS OTHERS' PAIN.` · `A WOMAN AND A BENT PIN.` · `DOCTORS WORK ON BELIEF.` · `HE LEAVES TALES TO THEIR TELLERS.` · then, large: `IT IMAGINES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a lemon, yellow and cold from the fridge, cut in half with juice on the board, and notice what your mouth does. Then bring to mind something you've been dreading this week, and notice your shoulders, stomach or jaw, though nothing in the room has changed. Name it quietly, it imagines, and come back to the breath.
The force of imagination. Montaigne's essay on how a picture in the mind can stir pain or ease in the body, starting with his own. Today's word.
Your line: it imagines. The picture can be vivid while the thing itself hasn't happened. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne turn to his essay on the force of imagination for its frank self-report: he describes how pictures in his own mind stir pain or relief in his body, and how others use that power.

notes: Chapter numbering: this essay is 1.21 in the path's outline (and in Villey's French edition); some English editions (Cotton/Hazlitt) number it 1.20. Confirm.
The pin story and the passage on leaving borrowed tales on the conscience of their tellers are paraphrased from memory of the essay; confirm both are in this chapter.
Latin tag 'Fortis imaginatio generat casum' ('say the scholars', in Montaigne); confirm wording and the pronunciation guide (ecclesiastical vs classical).
The practice uses the lemon exercise and a mild 'dread' check; no health claims are made. Montaigne's own claims about illness and cure are given as his, not as medical advice.
